# Plass

> Plass is a UI component library that ships one design language for two frameworks: `plass-ui` on npm for React, and `plass_ui` on pub.dev for Flutter. Both hold the same components under the same prop vocabulary and the same tokens, and the two version independently. The React package's behaviour and accessibility come from [Base UI](https://base-ui.com) primitives and its styling from [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com) v4; it ships as ESM only with type declarations included and has one runtime dependency (`@base-ui/react`). The Flutter package is built on `package:flutter/widgets.dart` alone — neither `material.dart` nor `cupertino.dart` — and has no dependencies at all. Both support dark mode out of the box.

The design language: **a Plass surface is a key of tinted glass resting on a clear sheet.** Every surface answers one question — is this pressed, or does it hold something? A thing that is pressed is tinted glass: a two-stop gradient at 135° whose ends are the two ends of a colour family at one lightness (indigo to azure, vermilion to rose), a drop shadow **tinted with that family**, and a bloom of light that follows the pointer. There is deliberately no specular highlight and no inset edge on a filled control — a gradient that turns carries the form, and a highlight over the top of it reads as lacquer. A thing that holds something is clear glass: translucent, `blur(22px) saturate(160%)`, a white hairline round it, and never dyed. A control never moves — there is no `transform` on press — it answers in light and depth: `brightness(1.05)` on hover and `brightness(0.95)` on press, with the elevation going one step up and one step down.

`elevation` defaults to **1 on a PlButton and 0 on a PlTextField**: a key rests on the sheet, a field is cut into it.

Every component draws from one shared prop vocabulary, so `size="md"` means the same thing everywhere:

```ts
type PlassSize = 'xs' | 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl';
type PlassColor = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'success' | 'warning' | 'danger' | 'info';
type PlassDensity = 'default' | 'compact';
type PlassVariant = 'solid' | 'glass' | 'ghost';
type PlassElevation = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3;
```

`color` is one of six semantic families, never an arbitrary value like `#3558ef`. Setup is `npm install plass-ui`, then one line in the app's CSS entry point — `@import 'plass-ui/styles.css';`. That file ships compiled, so Tailwind is not a requirement on the consumer's side. A project that already runs Tailwind v4 imports `plass-ui/tailwind.css` instead, which is the token sheet and registers the package as a Tailwind source, so consumers never write an `@source` of their own. On the Flutter side setup is `flutter pub add plass_ui` and nothing else — there is no stylesheet to import and no provider to install, and a component follows the platform's brightness until a `PlassTheme` overrides it. Neither package paints the page behind the glass: `--plass-bg-from` / `--plass-bg-to` in CSS and `tokens.bgFrom` / `tokens.bgTo` in Dart name that wash and leave the painting to the caller.

Ninety-eight components are released, across seven groups: display, feedback, inputs, layout, navigation, surfaces and transitions. The React package additionally exposes a small set of hooks and a few components that answer problems only the DOM has; those are listed at the end and are marked React-only where they appear. Every component is exported under a `Pl` prefix — `PlButton`, `PlTextField`, `PlAccordion` — because the bare names are the most-taken identifiers in the ecosystem, and because the design language is meant to be portable to other toolkits. The shared prop vocabulary keeps the `Plass` prefix (`PlassSize`), and so do the CSS tokens (`--plass-*`).

Documentation is available in English (served from `/`) and Korean (served from `/ko/`). The links below are the English pages; prefix any path with `/ko` for the Korean version.

## Guide

- [Getting started](https://plass.cdget.com/guide/getting-started): Install, the one-line CSS setup, what the bundled reset does, the Tailwind path, the page wash the glass needs under it, first component, dark mode via `data-theme` or a class, browser support.
- [Setting defaults](https://plass.cdget.com/guide/defaults): `PlassProvider` decides `size`, `color`, `density`, `locale`, `weekStartsOn` and the picker `labels` for everything under it, and `PlassTheme.merge` is the Flutter half (where `names` and `labels` are what a `locale` is, the framework shipping no `Intl`). Optional, and what it removes is transcription rather than configuration: the library is finished without one. It deliberately does **not** set `variant` or `elevation`, and that absence is load-bearing: `variant` names what a surface is *made of* and a button is `solid` while a card is `glass` because that is the arrangement, not an unset default; `elevation` is per-component semantics for the same reason, a control resting **on** the sheet at `1` and a field cut **into** it at `0`. One value for either would be a flattening rather than a default. Four layers of precedence, in the order a reader would guess: the component's own prop, then whatever set it is in (a `PlButtonGroup`), then the nearest provider, then the component's own default — and providers nest and **merge**, so a section that says only `density` keeps the `locale` from the provider above it. `labels` merges *under* each component's own, so an application translates the vocabulary once and one picker can still say something different. `usePlassDefaults()` reads what is in scope. `PlTable` is the one React component that does not read it, because it is kept out of the client graph on purpose; the Flutter build has no such boundary and no such exception. On the Flutter side the plain `PlassTheme` constructors **replace** the defaults in scope and `PlassTheme.merge` keeps the ones above — `DefaultTextStyle`'s own bargain, and there for its reason. It is not a theme: the colours, radii, blur and shadows are CSS custom properties, and a JavaScript copy of them would be a second source of truth.
- [Design language](https://plass.cdget.com/design/design-language): The tinted-glass rule and everything that follows from it — the three layers of a filled surface, why the gradient turns instead of shading, the three-strength glass ladder, the one inset shadow, tinted shadows, brightness-based press, the pointer-following interaction light, the size and radius ladders, and the implementation rules.
- [Colour](https://plass.cdget.com/design/color): The six semantic families as gradient sweeps, the three hand-picked tokens per family, why a family's colour does not change with the theme, the measured contrast table (every stop within 0.15 of 4.5:1), and how to override a family.
- [Right to left](https://plass.cdget.com/design/rtl): `dir="rtl"` on one element is the whole setup — no provider, no plugin, nothing to configure. Every padding, margin, border, radius and inset in the library is a **logical** property, which is the same rule the prop vocabulary follows (`PlassAlign` is `start | center | end`, a `PlSidebar` takes `side="start"`). What flips: the box model, text alignment, the chevrons that point along the reading direction, a `PlSwitch`'s thumb (off is the inline start, which is the right-hand end under RTL), and the drag *and* arrow keys of `PlPanes`, `PlSidebar`, `PlCarousel` and `PlScrollZone`. What does not: `PlassSide` — a tooltip above a button is above it in every writing direction — and any icon that is not directional. Direction is read in JavaScript in exactly three places, all of them where the thing being measured is physical too: a pointer's `clientX` grows to the right in both directions, and the moving indicator in `PlTabs`, `PlSegmentedButton` and `PlFloatingBottomNavigation` is placed from `offsetLeft`, so those three keep `left` on purpose — pairing a logical property with a physical measurement is what would actually break the direction. A package test renders in a real `dir="rtl"` document and reads every component's source for a physical utility not on a short documented list.
- [Prop conventions](https://plass.cdget.com/design/prop-conventions): What the shared props mean, the naming rules a new component is checked against, and the three state props with their focus and native-attribute behaviour.

## Examples

Whole screens rather than single controls — every one a live React composition of released components, with the source in `docs/.vitepress/demos/examples/`.

- [Admin dashboard](https://plass.cdget.com/examples/dashboard): A back office. A nav rail, a sticky app bar, four figures, a filter row, and a table with select-all, per-row menus, bulk actions behind a confirm dialog, and pagination. Shows what a size ladder looks like when a `PlTextField`, a `PlSelect` and a `PlDateRangePicker` share one row.
- [Landing page](https://plass.cdget.com/examples/landing): A marketing page. Hero, tabbed product views, a feature grid, a testimonial carousel, monthly/yearly pricing on a `PlSegmentedButton`, an FAQ accordion and a sign-up strip. The featured plan is marked with elevation and a chip rather than a saturated fill.
- [Sign-up](https://plass.cdget.com/examples/signup): A three-step form — account, code, profile — with real validation. Every control is a different component, which is where a shared vocabulary for `size`, `label`, `description` and `error` has to hold.

## Components

- [All components](https://plass.cdget.com/components/): Every released component on one page, each card a running preview rather than a picture.

### Display

- [PlImage](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/image): A picture and the two states a picture spends most of its life in. An `<img>` is one tag and it works, so what this adds is stated rather than assumed: the space is **reserved** before the picture arrives (`ratio`, the prop worth reaching for every time — without it there is nothing to reserve, because the box is however tall the picture turns out to be and nobody knows that until it lands), a failure is **drawn** rather than left as the browser's broken-image glyph and the alt text in a serif nobody chose, and the two are **one state machine**, so the placeholder is not still sitting behind a loaded picture and a changed `src` starts again rather than inheriting the last one's success. `alt` is required and `""` is a real answer — it marks the picture decorative. The `<img>` stays in the document while it loads, because an `<img>` that is not in the document never loads. `placeholder` replaces the skeleton (`null` draws nothing); `fallback` replaces the alt text, which is the default because it is the one thing certainly available and certainly describing what is missing. `preview` opens it over the page in a `PlOverlay` and is **off** by default — a picture that grows when you click it is a promise that there is more of it to see, and most are not making it; the trigger is disabled until the picture has arrived and is named after the picture rather than "Preview". `loading="lazy"` by default. There is deliberately no gallery and no next/previous inside the preview: a gallery is a list with a state of its own and composes out of what is already here.
- [PlList](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/list): A stack of rows — the list is a sheet, the rows are what is on it, and `size`/`density`/`dividers` are carried down by **context** rather than by `cloneElement`, which stops reaching a row the moment a caller `.map()`s their data. A row's shell is always an `<li>`; `onClick` or `href` puts a real `<button>` or `<a>` *inside* it, and `action` sits **outside** that pressable area, because a row that navigates and holds a toggle has two things to press. A chosen link gets `aria-current="page"`, a chosen button `aria-current="true"` — never `aria-pressed`, which would make it a toggle. `dividers` trades the sheet's padding and the rows' corners for edge-to-edge rules, drawn with `>li+li`. `role="list"` is written out because Tailwind's reset takes the bullets off and Safari takes the semantics with them. No Base UI primitive: a list is not a composite widget, and a listbox role on a page of links breaks a screen reader.
- [PlTable](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/table): A grid of data on a glass sheet. Takes `columns` and `rows` rather than markup, so the headings and the cells cannot drift apart; a column carries `key`, `header`, `width`, `align` and an optional `render`. `striped`, `hoverable`, `stickyHeader`, `caption`, `empty` and `onRowClick`. A clickable row keeps its `<tr>` semantics and gains a tab stop rather than a `role="button"`. Cell padding and alignment are inline styles, because host stylesheets style `td`/`th` by tag name at a specificity a utility class cannot outrank. It is generic in `Row` and so takes no `ref`.
- [PlAvatar](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/avatar): A picture of a person or a thing that is never an empty box, built on Base UI's Avatar — which owns the four-state load race. Three things can be drawn and one is at a time: the picture, then `children`/`initials`/initials derived from `name`, then a silhouette. The derivation is first-character-of-first-word plus first-of-last, and a single-token name gives one character, because two characters of a CJK name at 40px is a smudge. An avatar *is* the coloured thing, so its sheet takes the tint — but `variant` defaults to `ghost`, since a page of saturated circles is a page nobody can read a name off. `shape` is `circle` or the library's own fillet; there is no `density`. No status dot: that is a `PlBadge` with an avatar in it. A stack of them is a `PlStack` with avatars in it.
- [PlBadge](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/badge): A small mark in the corner of something else — unread mail on an inbox icon, a status dot on an avatar. With `children` it wraps the anchor in an `inline-flex` shell that adds no width, so a badged icon button still lines up with a bare one; without them it lays out inline as a standalone status pill. A count of `0` draws nothing unless `showZero`, and a number past `max` is capped with a `+` (a word is left alone). Omitting `content` gives a dot; `dot` forces one while keeping the content for screen readers. `label` is what turns "3" into "3 unread notifications". Pulled out of the corner with a **negative margin**, never a `transform`; `overlap="circle"` adds the inset a round anchor needs. It is the one component allowed to be a pill — a badge is a mark laid on a surface, not a surface. No role, no tab stop, no Base UI primitive.
- [PlBlockquote](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/blockquote): Somebody else's words, set apart from your own — an accent rule down the leading edge, the quote at a heading's scale with a paragraph's leading. `author` is a person and `source` a work, because `<cite>` is for the title of a work and never for a name; passing either turns the wrapper into a `<figure>` with the `<figcaption>` **outside** the `<blockquote>`, since a name inside it claims the speaker said their own name. Without one the wrapper is a plain `<div>`. **Nothing is drawn on the `<blockquote>` element itself** — a host stylesheet's `blockquote` rule outranks a utility, so the surface, the rule and the padding all live on the wrapper. The sheet is never dyed; the family reaches the rule and stops. `ghost` is the default.
- [PlBreadcrumb](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/breadcrumb): The trail of pages above the one being read — a named `<nav>` around an `<ol>` (order is the meaning). The **last step is the current one** on its own: it takes `aria-current="page"` and stops being a link even with an `href`, and a step that claims it with `current` takes the mark off the last one, since only one element may carry it. A step is a real `<a>` with `href`, a real `<button>` with only `onClick`, and a `<span>` with neither. `maxItems` folds the middle behind a `…` that unfolds in place — but only when the fold actually removes more than one step. Four named `separator`s, because the difference is meaning; the two that point turn back under RTL. `structuredData` emits a `schema.org` BreadcrumbList beside the markup (off by default, since a page may have only one), with every step in it including the folded ones, made absolute by `baseUrl`. `PlBreadcrumbItem` inherits `size` from the trail.
- [PlChip](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/chip): A compact token — a tag, a filter, a status, an entity plucked out of a list. The shell is always a `<span>`; `onClick` puts a real `<button>` *inside* it and `onDelete` adds a second one, because a button inside a button is invalid HTML browsers un-nest on parse — so both are real, focusable, separately reachable. `aria-pressed` reports `selected`. A chip is one step **down** the control ladder (a `md` chip is a `sm` control, 32px), because a chip is a token inside a row rather than a control the row lines up against. `variant` defaults to `glass`: a row of gradient keys has no primary action. `selected` moves one step up the variant's own ladder — and on `solid`, which has no opacity ladder, it casts the tinted lift instead. `count` rides on its own plate.
- [PlDivider](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/divider): A rule between two things. Base UI's Separator, so a real `role="separator"` with the matching `aria-orientation`. Like `PlTextLink` it has **no default `color`** — left out, the rule is the neutral hairline, the one visible on a page wash, a glass sheet and a card alike; the sheet's own white hairline vanishes on anything opaque. `children` breaks the line around a label and `textAlign` decides where it sits, with a fixed stub on the near side rather than a flex ratio. A string label is copied into `aria-label`, because `separator` is not a name-from-content role. `length` rather than `width`, because the long axis turns with `orientation`. No `variant` and no `elevation`: a divider is not a surface.
- [PlHighlight](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/highlight): Marks the words a reader is looking for inside text they were already reading. The component *is* the search: `query` takes a string, an array (longest term tried first, or `['data','database']` would mark `data` and orphan `base`), or a `RegExp` (copied, never mutated, global forced on). `caseSensitive` and `wholeWord` are props, not pre-computed offsets; whole-word is checked with two character tests rather than a lookbehind, which Safari only grew in 16.4. `children` is a **tree** — elements are walked into and cloned, so a match inside a `<strong>` is marked and the `<strong>` survives. The mark is a real `<mark>`, so marking eleven words tells a screen reader eleven things matter. `color` defaults to `warning`, the one family light enough to be a highlighter. No `size`: a mark is the size of the text it is inside.
- [PlHotKeys](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/hot-keys): A keyboard key, a combination of them, or the four movement keys as an inverted-T `cluster`. `Mod` is the token the rest exist for — the only one whose *meaning* changes with the platform (⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere); `os` overrides the detection for a page that must name a platform. Every glyph key carries its real name in a visually hidden box, because a screen reader announces `⌘` as "place of interest sign". The platform is resolved through `useSyncExternalStore` so a server-rendered page hydrates without a mismatch. `PlKbd` is exported as one cap. It displays a shortcut; it does not bind one.
- [PlIcon](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/icon): A glyph at a known size, in a known colour. The library ships no icon set — this gives whichever set the app chose the same two axes everything else has. The glyph is the `icon` **prop** rather than `children`, because size and colour are the two things you cannot reach once an icon set's element is a child. The box is `inline-flex` with `font-size` set to the same length as the box, so a px-authored `<svg>`, an em-authored one, a bare character and an `<img>` all come out the same size. `size` is its own 14/16/20/24/28px ladder, not the control heights. `color` defaults to **`inherit`**, the one component where it is not `primary`. Without `label` it is `aria-hidden` with no role; with one it is `role="img"` — there is no third case.
- [PlTimeline](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/timeline): A sequence of steps in the order they happen in, as a real `<ol>` — the order *is* the content. `active` is an **index**, not a value, because a timeline has no selection: everything before it is `complete`, the item at it is `current`, everything after `upcoming`. An item's index is never a prop; the timeline numbers its children as it walks them (through `Children.toArray`, so a conditional step that rendered nothing does not shift the count). Three states, three **axes** rather than three opacities: gradient, gradient plus a soft halo, hairline ring. The connector belongs to the item it *leaves*, so its colour says whether that step was reached, and it is one border edge so `dashed`/`dotted` are the browser's own. The current step takes `aria-current="step"`. `PlTimelineItem` inherits `size`/`density`/`orientation` and can override `status` and `color`.
- [PlStat](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/stat): One figure and what has happened to it. A row of these is the top of every dashboard, and the whole of what makes it worth a component rather than three `<div>`s is the **change**: a number on its own says what things are, and a number with a movement beside it says whether that is going anywhere. The colour of that movement is decided by `improvesWhen` and **not by the sign**, which is the one thing a naive version gets wrong — churn going up is not good news, and a green arrow on it is a dashboard lying to somebody; set `improvesWhen="down"` for churn, a bounce rate, a p95 latency, a cost. `value` takes a **node** rather than a number, deliberately: the currency, the grouping, the decimals and the locale are the page's decision and `Intl.NumberFormat` already makes it. `changeLabel` replaces the percentage for a figure that moved by a count while `change` still decides the arrow and the colour. `loading` draws a skeleton where the figure will be and holds the change back with it, because a movement beside a figure nobody has yet is a movement of nothing. It draws **no surface** — a figure sits in a `PlCard` — and the figure is `tabular-nums` so a row updating on a timer does not jitter. The arrow is `aria-hidden` and the sign is in the text, so colour is never the only thing carrying the direction.
- [PlTree](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/tree): A hierarchy opened one branch at a time. It takes its nodes as **data** rather than as children, the opposite of most of this library and the right way round here for one reason: a tree is recursive, and recursion written in JSX is a component every caller has to write for themselves (`PlTable` takes its columns the same way for the same reason). `expanded` and `selected` are separate arrays of ids and separate questions — opening a folder is not choosing it — each controlled or not. `selection` is `single` by default; `multiple` adds `aria-multiselectable`, and `none` makes it a **browser** rather than a chooser, where rows still expand and a click still reports through `onItemClick` but nothing stays lit. **`children: []` and `children: undefined` are different things**: the first is a branch that opens and shows nothing, the second is a leaf with no twisty at all — which is what makes a lazily-loaded tree possible. The keyboard is the ARIA tree pattern and is most of what makes this a tree rather than a nested list: **one tab stop** for the whole thing, following the focus rather than leading it so tabbing back in returns to the row you left; ↓/↑ walk the rows that are actually *visible*; → opens a branch and *then* steps into it, two presses, so a reader can open one without leaving the row that told them it was there; ← closes or steps out to the parent. A `disabled` row is `aria-disabled`, is skipped by the arrow keys and is left in place rather than removed, because a hierarchy with a hole in it is one nobody can read.
- [PlTypography](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/typography): The library's type scale on its own — ten `level`s from `h1` to `overline`, each setting the size **and** the element it renders as. Deliberately not called `variant`, which in this library names what a surface is made of. There is no `size` either: `level` is the size, and a second axis would allow an `h1` at `xs`. `render` breaks the tie when the scale and the semantics have to differ. `weight` is resolved in JS so exactly one `font-*` class is ever emitted — two of equal specificity would be decided by stylesheet order. `color` has **no default** (text inherits the page's ink), and `caption`/`overline` are muted. `lines` truncates at 1 and line-clamps above it, leaving the whole string in the DOM. `gutter` is off: a component that injects margins is one a layout has to fight.
- [PlTextLink](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/text-link): A link, in a sentence or on its own. No surface, no height, and — like nothing else in the library — **no default `color` and no default `size`**, because a link in a paragraph is the paragraph's colour with a line under it. `underline` is `'always' | 'hover' | 'none'` rather than a boolean. `newTab` sets `target`, merges `noopener noreferrer` into any `rel` the caller wrote, draws the external arrow and adds a visually hidden line for a screen reader. The component's class is doubled in CSS (`.plass-link.plass-link`) so a host page's `.prose a` cannot outrank it.
- [PlVisuallyHidden](https://plass.cdget.com/components/display/visually-hidden): Content for a screen reader and for nobody else — **React-only**, because what it works around is a DOM problem and Flutter answers it with `Semantics`. A one-pixel clipped box is the only form that is absent to a sighted reader and present to every other kind: `hidden` and `display: none` take the text off the accessibility tree along with the screen, and `opacity: 0` leaves a clickable ghost the size of the words. The library already reaches for the same rule inside a dozen components; this is it spelled once for the caller's own markup, and the ordinary use is naming a control whose whole label is a glyph (mark the glyph `aria-hidden`, or the control has two names). `focusable` puts the box back in the flow while anything inside it holds the focus, which is the skip-link case and cannot be done from outside — the clip is `position: absolute`, so revealing it means making it `static` again. It answers `:focus-within` rather than `:focus`, because what is tabbed to is the link *inside* the box. `render` swaps the `<span>` for the `<h2>` that structures a page for a screen reader or the `<div>` a live region wants; every native attribute passes through, `aria-live` included. No `variant`, `size` or `color`: nothing is drawn.

### Feedback

- [PlConfirmProvider](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/confirm): One dialog, asked for from anywhere under it and **awaited** — `if (await confirm({ title: 'Delete this project?', color: 'danger' })) …`, plus `alert` for the one-button form. The argument for a hook over a component is that the thing a caller has at the moment a question is warranted is a *click handler*, not a place in the tree: without it the same delete button needs a piece of state, a `<PlModal>` kept mounted beside it, and the work after the answer torn in half across a callback — three edits per button. It is `PlToastProvider`'s arrangement for the same reason. **Cancel holds the focus by default** (`initialFocus`), and that is the decision worth knowing: a confirm dialog exists to make somebody stop, and an Enter key landing on the destructive action defeats it; move it for a question whose yes is harmless. Questions asked while one is open are **queued** and the sheet's content changes rather than closing and reopening — the alternative is a promise nobody resolves, which is a hung button rather than a visible bug. A provider that unmounts with questions outstanding resolves them all `false`, so a route change does not leave a handler's `finally` unrun. `usePlConfirm` **throws** outside a provider rather than answering `false`, because a silent `false` is a delete button that quietly does nothing. Escape and a click outside answer no, never yes; `dismissible: false` is for the question that genuinely has to be answered.
- [PlEmpty](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/empty): The place where there is nothing. An empty list, a search with no results, a request that failed and a flow that finished are the **same arrangement** (a mark, a line, a sentence, a way out), which is why they are one component rather than four; what tells them apart is `color`: `secondary` is "nothing here yet", `danger` is "something went wrong", `success` is "you are done" — which makes the order-confirmed screen without a second component. It **draws no surface**, because an empty state is always inside something and a sheet inside a sheet is two sheets; `PlTable`'s `empty` prop takes a node, and this is the node it was waiting for. The part worth getting right is the **way out**: a screen that says "No projects" and stops is a dead end, and the same screen with a "New project" button is the best moment in the whole flow to offer one. The glyph is `aria-hidden` because the title says what it says. It has **no role of its own** on purpose — add `role="status"` when the emptiness is the *result* of something the reader just did, and leave it off for a list that was already empty when the page loaded.
- [PlPopconfirm](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/popconfirm): A question asked where it was raised rather than in the middle of the page. Built on `PlPopover`, so the popup is a `role="dialog"` named by its `title` and described by its `description`. The difference from `PlConfirmProvider` is not the words but **how much it interrupts**: a modal takes the page away and is right for deleting an account, while this appears against the row's own delete button, leaves the rest of the table readable, and puts a reader who presses Escape back exactly where they were. The rule of thumb is what happens if they answer by accident — if they can undo it, this is the one. `color` defaults to `danger` here and to `primary` on a `PlButton`, which is not an inconsistency: nobody reaches for a popconfirm to ask whether to save. `onConfirm` may return a **promise**: the button shows its loading state until it settles and the popup closes only if it *resolves*, so a failed request leaves the question up instead of pretending, and Escape is ignored while it runs. A rejection is caught and goes no further — keeping the question up is the whole of what the component owes a failure, and reporting what it means is the caller's job from inside `onConfirm`. **The focus lands on the confirming button**, the other way round from the modal and deliberately: a popconfirm is opened *by* the button it is asking about, so the reader has already said what they want once. There is no close button — two answers, two buttons.
- [PlOverlay](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/overlay): A sheet over the whole page that stops it being used — the scrim on its own, with whatever the caller puts on top. Built on Base UI's Dialog, so the portal, scroll lock, focus trap, inert page and focus restoration are the primitive's. No `variant` (the page is already taken; `tone` is the real question) and no `elevation` (the overlay *is* the plane everything floats above). `tone` is one axis of legibility: `scrim` matches `PlModal`'s backdrop exactly so the two never seam, `glass` is a lighter dim over a real blur, `solid` is opaque, `clear` draws nothing and still catches the pointer. **`dismissible` is off by default** — the other way round from a modal, because an overlay is not asking a question, it is saying *wait*. `label` has a default, since an overlay holding only a spinner still has to name itself. Opacity is the only thing animated.
- [PlToast](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/toast): A message that appears on its own, says what happened, and leaves — `PlToastProvider` once around the app, `usePlToast` anywhere under it. A **hook, not a component**: what a caller has when a toast is warranted is a click handler, not a place in the tree. Built on Base UI's Toast, which owns the timers and their pausing on hover and window blur, the `limit` queue, the swipe, the F6 hotkey and the live region. Everything about how a toast looks lives on the provider so the call site is only *what happened*; `color`/`variant`/`icon` per toast ride in Base UI's `data` slot rather than shadowing manager option names. `position` is one word (`bottom-end`), never a side plus an align, because a stack is only ever pinned top or bottom. `timeout: 0` for anything the reader must act on. `update` with a reused id is one toast that changed its mind. `promise` follows a request through loading/success/error. The × is hidden from the a11y tree on purpose — F6 is the way in. No `elevation`: a toast always floats at shadow 3.
- [PlTooltip](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/tooltip): A short label that appears when the pointer rests on something, built on Base UI's Tooltip — the delay, the group timeout, opening on focus but not a click-focus, Escape, and collision handling are all the primitive's. The whole component is a wrapper: the Trigger merges onto the child, so it adds no element and no tab stop. The plate is the **same floating sheet as the `PlSelect` popup** (`--plass-glass-press`, white hairline, shadow 3), not the filled key most libraries draw — a tooltip is a note about something, and a second kind of floating sheet on one screen is one too many. It wires `role="tooltip"` and `aria-describedby` itself, dropping the reference while closed. `PlTooltipProvider` shares one delay across a toolbar. `color` defaults to `secondary`. A tooltip **describes, it does not name** — an icon-only button still needs its own `aria-label`.
- [PlProgressBox](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/progress-box): A row of small glass plates that light up, and the shape that is about the material rather than the quantity — the same groove, corner and gradient the rest of the library is made of, so a loading state inside a Plass surface does not look borrowed. `count` (4 by default) is the number of plates; set it to the number of steps when the work genuinely has steps. With a value the plates fill in order and the leading one partially — each plate is a groove of its own, so four plates at 30% are one full plate and a fifth of the next rather than a quarter rounded off. Indeterminate they cycle, each held back by its own index, and what cycles is the fill's **opacity** and never its paint: `background-image` has no interpolation between a gradient and nothing. The plates never move. Plate size is the tick ladder a checkbox's box is on. Under reduced motion the wave is slowed rather than stopped.
- [PlProgressCircular](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/progress-circular): A ring that fills, for where there is no room for a bar. Takes `PlProgressLinear`'s props unchanged except `size`, which is diameter here rather than thickness — one component in three shapes is the claim, so they share a props table rather than three that would drift. The arc is the family's gradient rather than a flat colour, which costs a `<linearGradient>` of its own because an SVG stroke cannot be given a CSS one; the track under it is `--plass-track`, the same ink the bar's groove is. The value and the label sit **beside** the ring, not inside it: at `xs` the ring is fourteen pixels across and there is nowhere for "40%" to go. Indeterminate it draws a fixed quarter-arc and turns; with a value it holds still and the gap closes. The `<svg>` is `aria-hidden`, and under reduced motion the spin is slowed rather than stopped.
- [PlProgressLinear](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/progress-linear): A bar that fills, and the one indicator that shows *how much* is left at a glance. Built on Base UI's Progress, which owns `role="progressbar"`, the value and range attributes and `aria-valuetext`. The groove is `--plass-track` — the same neutral ink a `PlSlider`'s rail and a `PlSwitch`'s off track are cut in — and the segment over it is the family's gradient, so the filled run is the material the submit button is made of; the movement is on `width` because a gradient cannot be transitioned and a length can. No `variant`, no `density`, no `elevation`: one material, nothing to pad, and a groove does not float. `value` defaults to `null`, the indeterminate case, and the bar sweeps rather than sitting empty. `showValue` writes a percentage **of the range**, not of 100, unless `format` (`Intl.NumberFormatOptions`) says what the number means. Values outside the range are clamped. Under reduced motion the segment stops travelling and breathes in place rather than stopping.
- [PlSkeleton](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/skeleton): The shape of something that has not loaded yet — it reserves the space the real thing will take, which a spinner cannot. Three shapes sized off the ladders the real components use: a `line` is as tall as that step's type, a `circle` is exactly a `PlAvatar` at that size, a `rect` is a block. `lines` stacks real bars with real leading rather than one striped box, and draws the last one short the way a paragraph's last line is. Deliberately **not glass** — a flat tint with no blur, hairline, gloss or shadow, which also stops thirty placeholders asking for thirty backdrop filters. Unlabelled it is `aria-hidden`; `label` on the *one* that stands for the region makes it a `role="status"` with `aria-busy`. Under reduced motion the sweep becomes a colour pulse rather than stopping, since a still skeleton reads as an empty box that finished loading.
- [PlAlert](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/alert): A message about something that happened, set into the page it is about. An alert *is* the coloured thing, so its sheet takes the tint (unlike every container). `color` defaults to `info`, not `primary` — an alert is a note, not the primary anything. Each family draws its own shape as well as its own colour, so the severity does not depend on colour alone. `warning` and `danger` get `role="alert"`, the rest `role="status"`. The three shapes — bare line, line with glyph, headline plus detail — are one component with different slots filled. `onClose` is what makes the dismiss button appear; the component never hides itself.
- [PlModal](https://plass.cdget.com/components/feedback/modal): A sheet that takes the page away until it is answered, built on Base UI's Dialog — focus trap, scroll lock, aria wiring and focus restoration are all the primitive's. No `variant` and no `elevation`: a modal has already taken the page, and one that could be told to sit flat would be one that could be told to stop being a modal. `title` becomes the `<h2>`, `description` the accessible description, `actions` the end-aligned bottom row; `PlModalClose` is exported so an uncontrolled modal's Cancel button needs no state. The sheet caps its own height and scrolls only its body. Opening animates opacity alone.

### Inputs

- [PlButton](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/button): A control that runs an action. `variant` `size` `color` `density` `elevation`, plus `startIcon`, `endIcon`, `loading`, `readOnly`, `disabled`, `fullWidth` and `render`. `elevation` defaults to 1; `solid` is a pane of tinted glass whose gradient turns in hue, `glass` wears the family in its label, `ghost` has no surface until hovered. Every variant carries `.plass-glow`, a bloom that follows the pointer and flashes on press.
- [PlButtonGroup](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/button-group): A run of buttons that belong together. The corners that face a neighbour are squared off with logical properties, and `variant` `size` `color` `density` `elevation` `disabled` are stated once for the set — a group where one button is a size out is the failure it exists to prevent. The axes carry **no defaults of their own**: an axis the group does not state is one each button falls back to its own default on, and a button that states one itself still wins. Inheritance travels by context rather than by `cloneElement`, so it reaches a button wrapped in a tooltip, a fragment or a `.map()`. Only `glass` overlaps its keys by a pixel, because it is the only variant that draws an edge and two hairlines meeting is a seam twice the weight of every other line on the page. `orientation` and `fullWidth`. It is **not** a segmented control and has no value — that is `PlSegmentedButton`, which carries the roving focus and `radiogroup` semantics.
- [PlTextField](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/text-field): Single- or multi-line text input. The label, the description and the error are part of the component, wired together by Base UI's Field. `variant` defaults to `glass`; `solid` is a well cut into the sheet rather than a tinted pane, because a gradient under a caret is not legible. `error` also turns the field invalid, which re-points the whole slot family at `danger`.
- [PlCheckbox](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/checkbox): A single yes/no, built on Base UI's Checkbox. Clear glass with a hairline until ticked, then the family's gradient — the one place the library expresses a state by swapping the whole surface rather than shifting a step, because on and off are not two strengths of one material. No `variant`. The tick has its own size and radius ladders (`tickSizeClasses`, `tickRadiusClasses`), because a radius sized for a 40px control turns an 18px box into a circle. `label`/`description`/`error` from Base UI's Field; `indeterminate` gives the third state and `aria-checked="mixed"`.
- [PlCalendar](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/calendar): A month on the page rather than in a popup — the same grid a `PlDatePicker` opens, with the trigger and the popup taken away. That is the whole difference and it is the reason to have both: a picker is a *field* that happens to open a calendar and belongs in a form beside other fields, while this is a calendar that is not standing in for one — a booking page, an availability view, a date rail — where the grid *is* the interface. Because it is not a field it has no `label`, `description` or `error`; it keeps `name`, so a plain form can still submit what it holds, spelled the way the native input of the same shape submits (`YYYY-MM-DD`, then `YYYY-MM` and `YYYY`). `precision` is a **floor** rather than a starting view: at `month` the month grid is the last grid and pressing a cell in it answers, and the value is normalised to the 1st rather than to whichever day the cursor was resting on. `variant` is `glass` with a `PlCard`'s sheet and elevation; reach for `ghost` inside something that already draws one. There is no `density` — padding on a grid of forty-two squares is what stops them being squares — and no `readOnly`, because a grid whose every cell is inert *is* the disabled one, which `disabled` renders with the `inert` attribute rather than with a `disabled` on forty-two cells. `autoFocus` is **off**, the opposite of the picker's: a popup was just opened by somebody who wants to be in it, and a calendar in a page was not.
- [PlDatePicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/date-picker): One day, chosen from a calendar, on a `PlTextField`'s shell with a calendar glyph. **No date library and no translation files**: it is `Date` arithmetic plus `Intl`, so `locale` (a BCP 47 tag) supplies month and weekday names, AM/PM, the first day of the week, the order of the header's two buttons and the trigger's format. The remaining strings — "Today", "Previous month" — are one `labels` object with English defaults. The header is the point: the month and the year are each a button opening a grid of its own (twelve months, then twelve years), so any month is two clicks and any year is three; all three views share a width and a height so the popup never resizes. Six weeks always. **No typing into the trigger** — locale-dependent parsing cannot be done honestly without a date library. `minDate`/`maxDate` are day-granular; `shouldDisableDate` blocks individual days, which keep `aria-disabled` and their place in the roving arrow-key path. Cells are named with the full date from `Intl`. `name` submits a **local** `YYYY-MM-DD`, never `toISOString()`.
- [PlDateRangePicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/date-range-picker): A span between two days — `PlDatePicker` with a second end, and everything it says about `locale`, the header and the bounds holds unchanged. Two months by default, as **one calendar in two halves**: the left has no forward stepper, the right no back stepper, either header moves both, and a hole is left where a stepper is not drawn so the headings stay on one centre line. No outside days, because with six full weeks on both panels a day would otherwise be named twice in one popup. The band is drawn between the anchor and the pointer **before the second click lands** — that preview is the whole affordance. Backwards is the same range in the other order. The value is one `PlDateRange` object, never a tuple or two props; half a range is a real state and it lives inside the component, so a controlled caller is not handed one. `presets` take a function when they depend on today. `name` submits both ends under one name via `FormData.getAll`.
- [PlFilePicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/file-picker): A box you drop files on, or click to open the file dialog. No Base UI primitive — a dropzone is a div listening for four drag events plus an `<input type="file">`. It gets right the two things hand-rolled dropzones miss: a drag *depth counter* (dragenter/dragleave fire per child, so a boolean flickers) and applying `accept` to drops (the browser enforces it on its own dialog only). `maxFiles` counts against what is already held. `onReject` reports every refusal with a reason — `type`, `size` or `count`. The dashed edge is the one non-solid line in the library. `formatFileSize` is exported alongside it.
- [PlNumberField](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/number-field): A field that only holds a number, built on Base UI's NumberField — locale-aware parsing, clamping, press-and-hold repeat on the steppers and the hidden form input are all the primitive's. The shell is a `PlTextField`'s **to the pixel** (`fieldRestClasses`), so a quantity box in a form is the same object as the boxes around it, and `solid` is the well rather than a tinted pane. `steppers` is `end`, `split` or `none`; there is deliberately no stacked pair of half-height chevrons, because at `xs` each arrow would be under three pixels tall. `format` goes straight to `Intl.NumberFormat`, so the field can show `$1,240.00` while `value` stays `1240`. Shift takes `largeStep`, Alt `smallStep`. `allowWheelScrub` is off by default. `error` re-points the whole slot family at `danger`.
- [PlColorPicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/color-picker): A colour chosen by eye — a saturation square with a hue rail beside it, which is the arrangement every design tool has settled on because it puts every colour of a hue within one movement of the pointer. **The panel's state is HSV and it never leaves that model**, which is the decision the whole component turns on: through RGB every shade of black is the same colour, so a picker that re-parsed its own string would snap the hue rail to red the moment the pointer reached the bottom of the square. The string is derived from the model, and an incoming `value` only re-seeds it when it means something different — compared as a *colour*, not as a string, because `#FF0000` and `#ff0000` would otherwise re-seed on every render forever. `alpha` adds a third rail, `format` (`hex`/`rgb`/`hsl`) decides the notation on the way out and drops the fourth channel when the colour is opaque, and `swatches` puts a product's own handful of colours one click away — the built-in set is a plain spectrum plus greys rather than the library's six families, because those are semantic roles and a picker is asked for a colour, not a meaning. A chosen swatch's tick is black or white by **relative luminance**, so it does not vanish on yellow. `inline` draws the panel in the page with no trigger; otherwise it wears the same `PickerShell` the date pickers do. There is no colour library under it: `internal/color.ts` is a hundred lines of arithmetic.
- [PlCombobox](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/combobox): A field you can type into and also choose from, on Base UI's Combobox — the filtering and its collator, the popup, the `combobox`/`listbox` wiring, arrow-key navigation across both the list and the chips, and the hidden form input are all the primitive's. The shell is a `PlTextField`'s wearing a chevron, to the pixel, exactly as `PlSelect`'s trigger is. What differs is the text: it filters, and with `allowCustom` (on by default) it can **become** the value — offered as its own row at the end of the list rather than committed silently on blur, and a real option rather than a special case in the key handling. `multiple` turns the chosen values into `PlChip`s inside the field and keeps the input filtering after each, which makes the field's `size` a minimum height rather than a height, because chips wrap. Each chip's × is named after its chip. `items` is data, and a value is a `string` or a `number`, never an object. `emptyMessage`, `openLabel`, `clearLabel` and `removeLabel` are plain props with English defaults.
- [PlDateTimePicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/date-time-picker): A day and a time in one popup. The calendar is `PlDatePicker`'s and the columns are `PlTimePicker`'s, both unchanged, and they sit at exactly the same height because both read the `--p-cell` ladder — seven rows each — so the popup is one rectangle. The bounds are the one real difference from `PlDatePicker`: `minDate`/`maxDate` are read at **full precision**, so 09:30 on the 27th leaves the 27th selectable and greys out that morning in the clock, which is what a "not before now" rule needs. Picking a day leaves the clock alone and picking an hour leaves the day alone; with no day yet the clock writes onto today. `closeOnSelect` is false — a moment is two answers — so the footer carries a `Done`, and `Now` does not close. The trigger wears the calendar glyph alone. `name` submits a local `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM`, the shape `<input type="datetime-local">` uses.
- [PlTimePicker](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/time-picker): A time of day, chosen from **columns** rather than a dial — `role="listbox"` per unit, `option` rows with `aria-selected`, and a polite live region that reads the whole time back because three unlabelled lists of numbers say nothing on their own. `Intl` decides whether the clock is a 12-hour dial (which reads 12, 1, 2 … 11 and gains an AM/PM column) and what AM and PM are called. **Bounds are checked against the span a row stands for**, not one instant inside it: with `minTime` 09:30 the hour 9 stays available and the minute column greys out 00–25, where the naive check would hide the 9 and make half past nine unreachable. `hourStep`/`minuteStep`/`secondStep`, `showSeconds`, `shouldDisableTime(value, unit)`. `closeOnSelect` is **false** by default — a time is two answers — so the footer carries a `Done`. The value is a `Date`; `referenceDate` is the day a bare time is written onto and is frozen while mounted. The chosen row is revealed with `scrollTop` on its own column, never `scrollIntoView`. `name` submits a local `HH:MM`.
- [PlPagination](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/pagination): The strip of page numbers under a long list. Every button is a real `PlButton`, so it inherits the surface, the press signature and the height ladder. `count`, `page`/`defaultPage`, `onPageChange`, `siblingCount`, `boundaryCount`, `showArrows`, `showEdges`. The slot count stays constant as the window slides, and a one-page gap is filled with the page rather than an ellipsis. `getPageHref` turns every number into a real `<a href>` a crawler can follow; a handler alongside it cancels the navigation for a client-side router. Renders a `<nav>` around a `<ul>` with `aria-current="page"` and a live-region status line.
- [PlRadioGroup](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/radio-group): A set of options where exactly one is chosen, built on Base UI's RadioGroup — the set takes one tab stop and the arrow keys move within it. `PlRadioGroup` holds the set and `PlRadio` is one option; `size`, `color` and `readOnly` are inherited from the group, because a radio says nothing on its own. The dot is round, one of only two round things in the library. `orientation` defaults to `vertical`.
- [PlSegmentedButton](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/segmented-button): Two or more choices in one pill, exactly one taken. Built on Base UI's RadioGroup — `role="radiogroup"`, one tab stop, arrow keys, `aria-checked` — because a segmented button *is* "exactly one of these"; `aria-pressed` toggles would announce four independent switches. The groove carries `--plass-well`; on `solid` the tile is the family's gradient with its tinted lift, a key riding in a groove. The tile animates `left`/`top`/`width`/`height` measured off the chosen segment rather than a `transform`, so no label is resampled while it moves, and it is not mounted until something is chosen so the first choice appears in place. `PlSegment` inherits `variant`, `size` and `density` from the set.
- [PlSelect](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/select): One value chosen from a list, built on Base UI's Select. The trigger is drawn on `PlTextField`'s shell (`fieldRestClasses` in `internal/styles.ts`), so a select and a field in the same form are the same object; `solid` is the well, not a tinted pane. Options are `items` (data, not children) because the trigger has to know the labels before the popup opens. `label`/`description`/`error` come from Base UI's Field; `error` re-points the family at `danger`. The trigger is held open at the width of its longest label so choosing a shorter option does not shrink it. The popup is portalled and its positioner carries `.plass-portal`.
- [PlSlider](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/slider): A value chosen along a range, built on Base UI's Slider. The rail is a groove carrying `--plass-well` — the same inset shadow a `solid` field is drawn with — and the filled run is the family's gradient, with the thumb ringed in `--plass-surface` so it never dissolves into it. An array `value` makes it a range slider; there is no `range` prop. No `variant`: a slider is a groove and a key at once, and neither has a choice to offer. `label`, `description`, `showValue` (a function gets Base UI's localised strings), `orientation`.
- [PlSwitch](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/switch): An immediate on/off, built on Base UI's Switch. Off, the track is the groove carrying `--plass-well`; on, it is the family's gradient with its tinted lift. The thumb keeps `--plass-surface` in both states — it is the light on the track, not a second coloured object — and it is the one thing in the library that moves. No `variant`. `labelPlacement` puts the label before the track for a settings list. Choose it over `PlCheckbox` when the change takes effect immediately; if there is a Save button underneath, it should have been a checkbox.

- [PlIconButton](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/icon-button): A round button with a glyph in it and nothing else. It **is** a `PlButton` — the three materials, the elevation ladder, the pointer light, `loading`, `readOnly`, `disabled` and `render` all pass through untouched — with `children`/`startIcon`/`endIcon` replaced by one `icon`. Two things differ. `label` is **required**, because a button whose whole label is a drawing has no accessible name at all and "an icon button with no `aria-label`" is the commonest accessibility defect a component library ships; making it required is the only fix that survives review. And the shape is a disc, a deliberate exception to the house radius rule: that rule protects the flat run along the top and bottom edge where a line of text sits, and a glyph has no line of text, so a circle with one mark centred in it says the same thing by a different route. The radius is an inline style rather than a `rounded-full`, because PlButton already writes a `rounded-*` utility and two utilities setting one property resolve by stylesheet order.
- [PlRating](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/rating): A score out of five as a row of stars. An interactive one is a real **radio group** of hidden `<input type="radio">`s, one per choosable score under the fraction of a star it stands for — a rating *is* "exactly one of these", so it gets one tab stop, arrow keys, `aria-checked`, and a value in a form submission, none of which a row of buttons has. `precision` bounds what can be **chosen** and nothing else: a `value` of `4.3` draws as four stars and a third at every precision, because an average is not a choice. The fraction is the filled star laid over the empty one and clipped by width — nothing transformed, nothing scaled, so a half star is the left half of exactly the star beside it, and the clip runs from the inline start so it fills from the right under RTL. `readOnly` is a different component in the same clothes: no inputs at all, one `role="img"` with the score as a sentence, and it is the one `readOnly` in the library that does not drain the saturation — a row of grey stars would say the score itself was unavailable. Clearing rides on `click`, not `change`, because clicking an already-checked radio fires no change. `color` defaults to `warning`, the one place a component's default colour is chosen by what the object is rather than by what it means.
- [PlOtpField](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/otp-field): A row of one-character slots — a PIN, a texted verification code, an invite key — built on Base UI's OTP Field, which owns one hidden value behind however many inputs, paste spread across the slots from wherever the caret was, backspace stepping back a box, a click landing on the first empty slot, and `autocomplete="one-time-code"` so a phone offers the code from the message. `length` is clamped to 2–12: one box is a `PlTextField` and past twelve the row stops fitting a phone. `charset` (`numeric` by default, because that is what a texted code is and what puts a number pad on a phone) drops what it rejects rather than showing it, and reports through `onValueInvalid`. `groupSize`/`separator` split the row, and the separator is an `aria-hidden` span rather than a `role="separator"` — punctuation inside one value, not a break between two things. A slot has its own size, radius and type ladders: taller than it is wide so a row reads as places for one character each, a radius measured against the slot's *width* rather than a control's height (or `md` would be a pill), and type two steps up the control ladder, because a code is read off one phone and typed with the other hand. The shell is `PlTextField`'s, so `solid` is the well and not a tinted pane. The focus ring is `:focus` rather than `:focus-visible`, the one place in the library that distinction is deliberately dropped.

- [PlToggle](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/toggle): A button that stays down (`PlToggle`), and a set of them that share one state (`PlToggleGroup`). Built on Base UI's Toggle and ToggleGroup, which own `aria-pressed`, the controlled/uncontrolled pair and the roving tab index — one tab stop for a whole toolbar, arrow keys between the members. **Off is neutral**, and that is the whole difference from a `PlButton`: a button at rest is an action waiting to be taken, a toggle at rest is a state that is currently *false*, so accent ink on an unpressed toggle would be a lie. On, `solid` takes the family's gradient and the on-fill ink and the other two light the sheet and leave the label in the accent — the same two answers a `PlSegmentedButton`'s chosen segment gives. **The elevation does not move with the state**: "on" is a fact about the thing beside the toggle rather than about how far the key is off the page. It is not a `PlSwitch` (which changes a setting, where the change is the point) and not a `PlCheckbox` (which is an answer in a form, not a control). The group squares off the corners facing a neighbour exactly as a `PlButtonGroup` does, publishes the *same* context so a toggle picks up either kind of run, and reports an **array** in both the single and the multiple case. If the choice is a value rather than a state, that is a `PlSegmentedButton` or a `PlRadioGroup`.

- [PlTransfer](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/transfer): Two lists and the arrows between them — everything that could be chosen on one side, everything that has been on the other. The shape for a choice that is *long* (the columns in a report, the permissions on a role, the people on a channel), where a `PlCombobox` with forty chips in its field stops being readable and a list of forty checkboxes gives no answer to "what did I actually pick"; below about a dozen options one of those two is the smaller component. **Ticking is not choosing**, and that is the whole model: `value` is which side a row is on, ticks are which rows the next press moves, and the two are separate pieces of state. The order of `items` is the order *both* lists show, so a row does not move when it is sent across and back. Moving drops the ticks on what moved and keeps the rest — a row that has arrived is not still waiting to be sent, and a row the filter was hiding was never part of that press. `searchable` puts a filter over each list, folding case and combining marks (so `cafe` finds `Café`) through the same `searchText` a `PlCommandPalette` uses; a label that is a node rather than a string **stays**, because the alternative is a row disappearing from a filter it could never satisfy. Each heading carries an indeterminate select-all for its own list and a `ticked/total` count. A `disabled` item stays in the list and cannot be moved.

- [PlFieldset](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/fieldset): A group of controls that answer one question together, with a name on it. It draws **no surface**, deliberately: a group of fields is a *grouping* and not a sheet, and the sheet already exists — put it inside a `PlCard` or a `PlBox` when one is wanted. What it owns is the legend, the gap the controls stand at, and the one thing only a real `<fieldset>` can do — `disabled` reaches every control inside it, including ones a component three levels down rendered and never heard of it. The legend is a `<div>` pointed at by `aria-labelledby` rather than a `<legend>`, which is Base UI's decision and the one that makes the group a normal flex container: a rendered `<legend>` is lifted out of its fieldset's content box by every browser, so a `gap` would put no space under it. The browser's own border, padding and margin are undone, and `min-w-0` with them — a fieldset is `min-width: min-content` by default, which is what makes one holding a wide table refuse to shrink.
- [PlForm](https://plass.cdget.com/components/inputs/form): A `<form>` that knows which of its fields is wrong. On its own a page of `PlTextField`s validates one field at a time and a failed submit leaves the reader to find the red one; what this adds is the part that has to be owned *above* the fields — a submit collects every field's validity at once, focuses the first that failed, and `errors` puts a server's answer back on the field it belongs to (by `name`) rather than in a banner at the top, clearing it as soon as that field changes. `validationMode` is Base UI's own three under its own spelling, defaulting to `onSubmit`, which is the only one that does not tell somebody their email is wrong while they are still typing it. It is **not a form library**: no schema, no resolver, no field array — a project that has those hands their result to `errors`, which is the seam this is built around. It draws no surface either; a form is a stack of controls and the sheet is a `PlCard` when one is wanted. Every field component in the library renders a `Field.Error` **whether or not it was given one**, so a message that came from the browser's own constraint validation or from a `PlForm`'s `errors` has somewhere to appear.

### Layout

- [PlAspectRatio](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/aspect-ratio): A box that keeps a proportion whatever width it is given, and draws nothing at all — no sheet, no hairline, no shadow. `ratio` is CSS's own `aspect-ratio` untranslated, so a number or a `'16 / 9'` reaches the property as written. `fit` is the one convenience on top: a direct `img`, `video`, `canvas`, `svg` or `picture` is stretched to the box and then fitted, which is the pair of declarations every use would otherwise start with — an `iframe` takes the sizing and not the fit, because an embed lays its own content out. `rounded` cuts the corners to the `size` step of the house ladder, and the box clips either way, since a `cover` image that spilled out of its proportion would leave the component reserving space rather than holding anything to it. The only shared axis is `size`, and it is the size of the sheet: a layout component that drew a surface would make a proportion a visual decision.

- [PlContainer](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/container): Horizontal breathing room and optionally a measure, drawing nothing itself — the outermost element on a page is the one thing that must not decide what the page looks like. `maxWidth` is the breakpoint ladder in `rem` (`xs` 30 · `sm` 40 · `md` 48 · `lg` 64 · `xl` 80) rather than a framework's own container scale, so a container's `lg` and an `lg:` utility change at the same width; `none` is the default, because the gutter is the job and a measure is a second decision. The gutter is the **sheet** padding track, not the control one: what is inside is a page, and a page's margin from the window is a card's margin round a paragraph. `padded={false}` gives the gutter up and keeps the measure and the centring, which is what a container nested in one that already pads wants. `centered` is inert while `maxWidth` is `none` — with no measure there is nothing left over to centre in. It has nothing to do with the grid: a container holds one as happily as it holds a paragraph, and a grid needs no container around it.
- [PlGrid](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/grid): A twelve-column row (`PlGrid`) and the cells in it (`PlGridItem`), drawing nothing — no sheet, no padding, no typography, and no `variant`/`color`/`elevation`/`size`/`density` on either. `span`, `offset`, `columns` and the three spacings are all `PlassResponsive<T>`: a bare value applies everywhere, a map applies each entry from its own breakpoint up, and the breakpoints are Tailwind's own so a Plass grid and an `md:` utility change together. A span wider than the row is clamped to it rather than overflowing; `offset` is space pushed in **ahead** of a cell rather than an absolute position, so document order stays reading order. `spacing` is Tailwind's scale (`4` is `1rem`, fractions allowed) and the gutter comes out of the cell, so two halves plus one gutter is exactly the row. It is a flex row with a percentage width per cell, not `display: grid` — the only shape where a cell can carry a start offset with no line number and where the row can be told not to wrap. The column count and both gutters reach a cell as **inherited custom properties** rather than through context, because a media query can change one without React hearing about it; the width arithmetic itself is real CSS in `styles.css`, since a class name assembled at runtime is one Tailwind never sees. Nesting is a grid inside a *cell*.
- [PlFlex](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/flex): A row or a column and the gap between the things in it — the layout box with no arithmetic in it, where a `PlGrid` divides a row into twelve and a `PlStack` overlaps what it is given. **React-only**, because `Row`, `Column` and `Wrap` are already in `package:flutter/widgets.dart` and already take a `spacing`; the half worth having in Dart is the responsive axis, and that is a `LayoutBuilder`. `direction` is `PlassResponsive<PlassOrientation>` and **resolves in CSS** — one `--p-dir-*` slot per rung the caller named, cascaded by the same `@variant` blocks a grid’s columns use — so `{ xs: 'vertical', md: 'horizontal' }` is a form that stacks on a phone and lines up on a laptop with a server render that is already right at every width, no listener and no re-render. `reverse` folds into that same slot rather than taking one of its own, which is why it is not responsive: one custom property carries the whole answer, so a breakpoint changes the axis without restating which end it starts from. It is a **painting order** and moves nothing in the DOM, so it is for an arrangement and never for content whose order is the information. `spacing` is Tailwind’s scale (`4` is `1rem`, fractions allowed) and the same one a grid’s gutter is; `rowSpacing`/`columnSpacing` take one axis each. `wrap` is **`false`** by default, unlike a grid’s, because that is what a flex box already does and the opposite default would silently reflow a toolbar somebody sized to fit. `inline` puts the box in a line of text. It draws nothing and takes no `variant`, `color`, `size`, `density` or `elevation`: a flex box is the arrangement of the surfaces inside it.
- [PlStack](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/stack): Things piled up, overlapping — faces, cards, thumbnails, whatever it is handed. It replaced `PlAvatarGroup`, which was this with one kind of child written into it. **The overlap is real layout rather than a transform**, and that is the whole component: a translated pile is laid out one item wide, paints outside its own box, and every element after it is placed against a size the reader never sees — so a negative margin in React, and a render object of its own in Flutter, where `EdgeInsets` and `Flex.spacing` both assert they are not negative. Five 32px items at 10px of overlap measure 120x32 `horizontal`, 32x120 `vertical`, 120x72 `diagonal`. A flow only overlaps on the axis it flows along, so `diagonal` flows across and takes its vertical `drop` per item — which is also why it is a **fan** rather than a true 45°: the horizontal advance is `item width - overlap`, and a component taking arbitrary children does not know that width. `max`/`total`/`overflow` handle the ones that did not fit, and `overflow` is a **function** because the hidden count *is* the item. `front` states the stacking order rather than inheriting the DOM's, `scaleStep`/`opacityStep` compound away from whichever end is in front, and `ring` draws the surface-coloured hole a near item is cut out of — on the element you passed, so it takes that element's shape. What it gives up is the group context: a pile that accepts arbitrary children cannot set an axis on them, so `size` and `color` come from a `PlassProvider` around it.
- [PlShow](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/show): Content at some widths and not others — `from`, `until`, or both as a band. It decides in **CSS**, and that is the whole component: a media query answered in JavaScript is `false` on a server and on the first frame a browser renders, so a `useMediaQuery` and a ternary draw the wrong half of a responsive layout and throw it away, which is a flash on every page load rather than an edge case. It is also the only way to gate on width for a project that imports `plass-ui/styles.css` and has no Tailwind of its own. While showing it is `display: contents`, so it is **not a box** — children take part in the surrounding layout exactly as they would without it, and a `className` carrying a margin or a width lands on nothing. Hiding is `display: none`, which takes the subtree off the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, so nothing is read twice — but **both halves are in the document**; for a subtree that fetches, is expensive, or must not mount at all, `usePlBreakpointValue` mounts one and pays the server's `xs` first render. `until` is exclusive, so `until="md"` and `from="md"` are the two halves of one decision. There is no `xs` bound and no `PlHide`.
- [PlPortal](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/portal): Children rendered somewhere else in the document — `createPortal` plus the three things a library has to add, and the first is the only real reason to reach for it. **It carries `plass-portal`**, the class every portalled surface here already lands with, because a portalled subtree leaves whatever element a host had scoped its CSS reset to and the class is how that host finds it again; it is a hook and not a style, and the library declares nothing for it. **It renders nothing until it has mounted** — there is no `document` on a server, so the shipped HTML never contains a portalled subtree and neither does the hydrating render, which is what a portal *is* rather than a limitation, so anything that must be in the server's HTML does not belong in one. **`container` is resolved after mount**, which is what lets it be a ref or a `getElementById`: the element a portal targets is usually one React has not created yet when the prop is written, so reading it during render would get the wrong answer every time; an element or a fragment is taken as it is, anything resolving to nothing falls back to `document.body`. What it does **not** carry is the colour scheme — the stylesheet answers to a `.dark`/`[data-theme]` on an *ancestor*, and a portal to the body has left every ancestor it had, so a themed subtree goes back to the page's; `container` pointing inside the theme is the fix, and it is the same fix the library's own popups need. React context does cross it, because the tree context is read from is the React one, so a `PlassProvider` above still decides `size`, `color`, `density` and `locale`. `disabled` renders in place and must be decided **once, at mount** — flipping it remounts the subtree and throws away a half-filled form or a playing video. `render` swaps the wrapper for whatever the target accepts (`<li>`, `<tbody>`). It does not trap focus, block the page or close on Escape: those belong to the thing being portalled. **React-only** — an `overflow: hidden` ancestor and an inescapable stacking context are DOM problems, and Flutter's answer is the `Overlay` every app already has.
- [PlSidebar](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/sidebar): A column beside the page's content, and a drawer once the window is too narrow to hold one — **two presentations of one panel**, so a caller never swaps components at a breakpoint and the children exist once either way rather than being rendered twice for a screen reader to read twice. A real `<aside>`, the `complementary` landmark, and it is named by default (`label`) because two unnamed sidebars are two regions called "complementary". Which of the two shapes is showing is a media query answered **in CSS for the first paint and in JavaScript from then on**: the markup a server sends is the column, so the class that hides it below the breakpoint is what stops a phone drawing a full-width sidebar and throwing it away, and `matchMedia` is what decides, once there is a window to ask, that the drawer should exist at all. `resizable` lets the inner edge be dragged; the width is written **straight onto the element** rather than into state, because nothing in the tree depends on it but one declaration and a `setState` per pointer move would re-render every row in the panel. The handle straddles the edge rather than sitting inside it — a one-pixel hairline is a one-pixel target — and is a real `role="separator"` tab stop the arrow keys move, with a key press firing `onResizeEnd` because it is a whole gesture on its own. `sticky` is on and costs nothing when it is not needed. `PlSidebarTrigger` is the hamburger that brings a collapsed one back: it lives in a `PlHeader`'s `brand` slot, is hidden by the *same* media query rather than by state, and renders nothing outside a `PlPageLayout`, where there is no sidebar it could be talking about.
- [PlFooter](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/footer): The sheet at the end of a page — a real `<footer>`, which at the top level of a document is the `contentinfo` landmark: the region a screen reader offers as "the site's own information" and a search engine reads the copyright, the address and the site map out of. **It has no slots on purpose**, which is the whole difference between it and `PlHeader`: a header's three regions are a fixed arrangement worth writing once, and a footer's content is four columns on one site and one line on the next, so a component that guessed at the arrangement would be one every second site fights. What it decides is the sheet — the surface, the gutter, the hairline and whether it stays in reach. `position` defaults to **`static`**, the opposite of a header's, because a footer is the end of the document and is reached by scrolling to it; `sticky` and `fixed` are for the bar that has to stay in reach (a form's save row, a cookie notice), and a `PlPageLayout` reserves what a `fixed` one takes out of the flow. `divider` is on by default and rules the **top** edge, which is the one that faces content. The sheet is never dyed, and `maxWidth` holds the content to `PlContainer`'s own ladder while the sheet still spans the window.
- [PlHeader](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/header): The bar across the top of a page — a real `<header>`, which at the top level of a document is the `banner` landmark and is the whole reason this is a component rather than a row of `<div>`s. Three slots (`brand`, `children`, `actions`) as props rather than sub-components, for `PlCard`'s reason: the arrangement is fixed and what a caller decides is what goes in each. `align="center"` gives **both ends an equal share** rather than centring the middle in the space left over, because a logo one character longer would otherwise move the navigation. `position` defaults to `sticky` (in the flow, so nothing has to be padded out of its way); `fixed` is answered by a `PlPageLayout` reserving its height. The sheet is never dyed and `divider` is on by default — a translucent bar pinned over a scrolling page has content passing under it at every moment. `size` is a **floor**, not a height: `md` is 64px, a 40px control with 12px either side, and a bar whose content wraps grows and keeps its padding. `maxWidth` holds the row to `PlContainer`'s own `rem` ladder while the sheet still spans the window, so the logo and the first paragraph under it sit on one edge. It is not a `PlToolbar` with a tag on it: a toolbar is a row of controls with no floor, no measure, no brand slot and no place in a layout. Inside a `PlPageLayout` it registers itself so a sidebar knows how far down to start; outside one it is simply a bar.
