- [PlPageLayout](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/page-layout): The skeleton a page is hung on — a header, a footer, one sidebar or two, and the content between them — and what it is really for is the **landmarks**: a page of `<div>`s is one undifferentiated region to a screen reader, and the same page built out of `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<aside>`, `<main>` and `<footer>` has a table of contents. It draws no surface, contributes exactly one element plus the `<main>` and the skip link that jumps to it, and draws no gutter or measure either — that is `PlContainer`'s job, put one inside. The arrangement is flexbox and media queries rather than JavaScript, so it is right in the first frame the browser paints and right with scripting off. `headerSpan`/`footerSpan` decide which of the bar and the columns takes the top corner: `full` is a website, `content` is an application, and the footer answers it separately. `scroll` is `page` (the document scrolls, the address bar hides on a phone, the back navigation restores the position) or `content` (the layout is exactly one screen and only the middle scrolls). The one thing measured is the two bars' heights, written onto the root as `--p-layout-header`/`--p-layout-footer` plus an `-inset` each, because a `sticky` bar takes nothing out of the flow but is still across the top, while a `fixed` one has to be reserved for — and which it is is read off the element's own `position` rather than plumbed through a prop. A bar is measured exactly when it registers, which `PlHeader` and `PlFooter` do. The skip link is on by default, clipped to a pixel rather than hidden so the Tab key can find it.
- [PlPanes](https://plass.cdget.com/components/layout/panes): A set of regions (`PlPane`) with draggable handles between them, sized in **fractions** written as `flex-basis: calc((100% − gutters) × fraction)` — which is the decision the whole component follows from: a split described as a percentage survives a window resize with nothing running, so it measures itself only twice, on mount and at the start of each drag. That measurement is a `ResizeObserver` rather than one read, because a split inside a closed accordion is zero wide when it mounts. `defaultSize`/`minSize`/`maxSize` take a number as a percentage and a string as an absolute length (`'240px'`), and they are read by the **split** rather than the pane — a pane cannot know what "half" is. Handles are interleaved by the component, so the children are just panes; what is drawn is a hairline and what can be **grabbed** is a track around it, the same split a scrollbar makes. A handle is a `role="separator"` with `aria-valuenow`, a tab stop while `resizable`, and moved by the arrow keys — a key press fires `onResizeEnd` because it is a whole gesture on its own. A drag takes the page's text selection away (as `-webkit-user-select`, the only name WebKit implements) rather than calling `preventDefault`, which would stop the browser focusing the handle; and it tears itself down on unmount, because the `pointerup` that would have ended it never arrives after a route change.

### Navigation

- [PlBottomNavigation](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/bottom-navigation): A row of destinations held against the bottom edge of the window. A `<nav>` of real links or buttons and deliberately **not** a `role="tablist"`: a tab list owes a keyboard reader one tab stop and arrow keys, and a screen reader a panel per tab, and a bottom navigation switches what the *page* is — claiming the role without the behaviour is worse than never claiming it. What it claims instead is `aria-current="page"`, never `aria-pressed`. `position` defaults to `fixed`, against the `static` a layout component takes, because that is what this component is; only a `static` bar has corners, since one spanning a window edge has nothing behind them. `labels` (`all` · `selected` · `none`) never changes the bar's height — the named item is always the tallest — and an **undrawn name is still in the document**, because a glyph on its own has no accessible name. `safeArea` moves the items clear of the home indicator while the sheet keeps reaching the bottom of the screen, so no stripe of page shows under the glass. The sheet is never dyed; the family is carried by the one item that is current. An item with an `href` is a real `<a>` (long-press, status bar, crawler) and loses that `href` when disabled, since `disabled` is not a state an `<a>` can be in.
- [PlFloatingBottomNavigation](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/floating-bottom-navigation): A row of round destinations floating clear of the bottom edge — a capsule of clear glass with a key of tinted glass riding in it. The other half of `PlBottomNavigation` and a separate component rather than a `floating` boolean, because half the props on each would mean nothing on the other: that bar is *attached* to the window edge (full width, a hairline against the content, flat), and this one is not part of the page at all, which is where the capsule, the gap, the `elevation` of **2** and the pill corners all come from. `rounded-full` is one of the very few pills the library allows, for the reason a segmented button's groove is: the house fillet is about a sheet with its corners cut, and a sheet that is not on anything has no corners to cut. Every destination is a disc with a glyph and **no name drawn** — the name is required and lives in a clipped box, because a row of glyphs with no accessible names is the defect `PlIconButton`'s `label` exists to prevent. The strip the capsule is centred in spans the window and takes no pointer events; only the capsule takes them back, or a transparent band would swallow every press along the bottom of the page. The focus ring on a disc is offset rather than flush, the one place in the library that differs: a flush ring on a circle is the circle's own edge thickening.
- [PlCommandPalette](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/command-palette): Everything an application can do, behind one field — the shape a keyboard-first product takes once it has more actions than a menu bar can hold, where a reader types what they want instead of remembering where it was put. It is **not a `PlMenu`** (a menu is a short list in one place, and every row is visible before you look for it) and **not a `PlCombobox`** (what comes back is not a value, it is something happening). Base UI's Autocomplete owns the list — the single highlight the pointer and the arrow keys share, `aria-activedescendant`, Enter running the highlighted row — and its Dialog owns the sheet, the scrim, the focus trap and returning focus to wherever the reader was. Filtering is done **before** the list rather than by the primitive, so a group heading can be drawn from the same array the rows come out of; each command's haystack is folded **once per list** rather than once per comparison, because `normalize` on every command on every keystroke is the cost that makes a palette feel slow. `keywords` are matched and never drawn — the name somebody else's product gives the same command. `shortcut` is displayed with `PlHotKeys` and **not bound**; the one keystroke the component does bind is its own opener, read with the same `Mod`-aware vocabulary it draws, so the label on the screen and the key that works are spelled the same way. The query is dropped on the way **out**, so the sheet never flashes the last search as it fades.
- [PlMenu](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/menu): A list of actions that appears when something is pressed, built on Base UI's Menu — the `menu`/`menuitem` roles, roving focus, typeahead, `Esc`, outside-click, focus restored to the trigger, and submenus that open on hover with a safe triangle. The rows are **composed, not passed as data** — the opposite of `PlSelect`, and deliberately: a select's options are values a caller already has, a menu's rows are code, and data would mean an `items` type with a variant per row shape. `PlMenuItem` renders a real `<a>` when given an `href`; `PlMenuCheckboxItem` (tick) and `PlMenuRadioItem` (dot) both default to **staying open**, against a plain row's `closeOnClick`. A row's `color` is a *branch* rather than an appended class, because two utilities of equal specificity resolve by stylesheet order and an appended accent would silently do nothing. Rows carry no focus ring — Base UI moves focus onto the highlighted row, so the tint is the indicator and `data-highlighted` is what lights it, which makes the keyboard and the pointer light the same row. The popup is `PlSelect`'s popup to the pixel and animates **opacity only**: a menu that slides in has moved the row you were reaching for. There is no `variant` (a popup that took the pointer has already answered that question) and no `elevation` (it is fixed at 3, because a menu genuinely floats). `PlContextMenu` is the same surface opened by a right-click or a long press, taking the rows as `content` and the region as `children`.

- [PlBackTop](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/back-top): The way back up, once there is a way back up to want. It is **hidden until it is useful** and that is the whole design: a button pinned to the corner of every page from the first paint is one more thing covering the content, and on a page too short to scroll it is a control that does nothing. It appears at `visibilityHeight` (400 by default, roughly one screen on a laptop — the point at which scrolling back stops being something a reader would just do), and while it is out of reach it is **`aria-hidden` and out of the tab order** rather than merely faded, because a control a reader can tab to and cannot see is worse than one that is not there. `target` is the window by default and takes a ref for a panel that scrolls inside the page; `floating={false}` keeps the appearing and the scrolling and gives up the corner. The scroll is smooth and **not** under `prefers-reduced-motion` — a page that flies past a reader who asked for less movement is the exact case that setting exists for, so it jumps instead. The position is read once on mount as well as on every scroll, so a page restored halfway down has the button already there. A caller's own `onClick` runs first and can `preventDefault()` to take the reader somewhere other than the top. Everything else is a `PlIconButton`'s.
- [PlStepper](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/stepper): A process the reader is moving through, and where they are in it. It draws the **same rail** a `PlTimeline` does and shares it in the source (`internal/steps.ts`), because a haloed bullet must not mean two things; the difference is what each is *for*. A timeline **reports** — an `<ol>` of text about a sequence that already happened, nothing on it can be pressed. A stepper **is** the sequence: the steps are buttons, the current one owns a panel, and pressing one moves the reader. `active` is an **index** rather than a value, exactly as a timeline's is, because a stepper has no selection. `linear` is on by default and is what makes it a process rather than a row of tabs — the third step of a sign-up cannot be filled in before the second — while a step *behind* the reader is always reachable, since going back to correct an answer is the whole reason a stepper is not a wizard with one door. Horizontal puts the panel under the rail; **vertical puts each panel inside its own step**, which is the reason to lay one out vertically at all. `status` overrides where the sequence says a step is, for the one that failed validation while the reader was three steps on; `color` on that step says why. `optional` takes `true` for the word or a node to translate it — one prop rather than two. It is deliberately **not** a `role="tablist"`: a tab list owes a keyboard reader one tab stop and arrow keys, and claiming the role without the behaviour is worse than never claiming it; each reachable step is its own tab stop, and a step that cannot be reached is not a button at all rather than a disabled one. **The steps have to be its own children** — it numbers them by walking them, so a wrapper component returning three steps is one child holding three.
- [PlMenubar](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/menubar): The strip of words at the top of an application — File, Edit, View — each of which opens a menu. What makes it a *bar* rather than a row of separate menus is what happens once one is open: moving along the strip walks through the others instead of closing the one you left, and the arrow keys move between the menus as well as inside them. Base UI owns that and the `menubar` role. A `PlMenubarMenu` has no `size`, `color` or `density` of its own — all three belong to the bar, which is the only place they can be set once and hold for every menu on it — and the rows inside are the same `PlMenuItem`, `PlMenuSeparator`, `PlMenuGroup` and `PlMenuSubmenu` a `PlMenu` takes, because it **is** the same menu. The trigger sits a rung **below** the control ladder at every step and uses the compact padding track even at `density="default"`: a menu bar is a strip of words, not a row of buttons, and sized as controls `File Edit View` would make the bar taller than the toolbar it is drawn on. It draws **no surface**: a menu bar sits on something, and a sheet under a strip that is already on a sheet is two sheets. The open menu is marked in colour and nothing else — the word does not move and the strip does not change height.
- [PlNavigationMenu](https://plass.cdget.com/components/navigation/navigation-menu): A site's navigation — a row of destinations, some of which open a panel of more of them. The difference from a `PlMenu` is what the rows *are*: a menu holds actions, so its rows are `menuitem`s and the whole thing is a widget that traps the arrow keys; this holds links, so it is a `<nav>` full of real `<a>`s, which is what puts them in the link list, on the status bar and in a crawler's index. Reach for a menu when the row **does** something and for this when the row **goes** somewhere. An item with an `href` and no children is rendered as a link and announced as a destination; one with children is a trigger with a panel, and the difference is not cosmetic. Base UI keeps **one panel open at a time and resizes it between items** rather than closing and reopening, which is what makes crossing the row read as one surface rather than three. The row carries **no surface at rest** — the words are the page's own, and five bordered boxes across the top of a site is a toolbar rather than a navigation. The panel is `PlMenu`'s popup to the pixel and animates opacity and its own measured size, never a slide: a panel that slid in would drag a page's worth of links across the screen. `columns` lays a panel out in a grid; `PlNavigationMenuLink` is one row in it, with a `title` and an optional muted `description`. A `target` other than this tab has `noopener noreferrer` **merged** into whatever `rel` was asked for, through the same `internal/link.ts` `PlTextLink` uses.

### Surfaces

- [PlCard](https://plass.cdget.com/components/surfaces/card): The sheet everything else on a screen is grouped onto. `title`, `subtitle`, `headerAction`, `footer` and the body are slots rather than sub-components. `elevation` defaults to 1 — a card lies on the page wash. `dividers` scores the sheet instead of spacing its sections; `padded={false}` gives up the inset for full-bleed content; `interactive` lifts the sheet under the pointer, which is the one `transform` in the library, allowed because a card holds content rather than being pressed. It adds no role — a clickable card takes a real element through `render`.
- [PlChatBubble](https://plass.cdget.com/components/surfaces/chat-bubble): One message in a conversation. `side` is `start`/`end`, never them/me or left/right, and it decides only the row direction and which corner is cut short — a flat **4px** written out rather than a step down the radius ladder, because 8px against 16px is not a difference anyone reads as meaning something. That cut is the library's one piece of chat vocabulary: it does a tail's job without hanging a triangle off a sheet cut with a straight edge. A bubble *is* the coloured thing, so `solid` floods it — and `variant` is deliberately **not** tied to `side`, since which column is filled is a product decision. Five delivery states, of which only `read` and `failed` carry colour; the mark is drawn and the word lives in a clipped box. `typing` swaps in three dots that change colour without moving, leaving `children` intact. `media` is edge-to-edge (the padding lives on the sections), and the link card's surface is mixed from `currentColor` so it works on a filled bubble and a bare one alike. `actions` fade in on hover or focus, and are always visible on touch. No role of its own: the thread is the page's list.
- [PlTabs](https://plass.cdget.com/components/surfaces/tabs): One set of panels, one of which is shown, built on Base UI's Tabs — roving focus, the arrow keys on the bar's own axis, the `tab`/`tabpanel` roles and the `aria-controls` wiring. `PlTab` and `PlTabPanel` are written as siblings and sorted apart by the component; there is no `PlTabList` to remember. `activateOnFocus` is off by default, because automatic activation fires a request per tab walked past once a panel fetches. `variant` `glass` is the classic rule-and-indicator bar; `solid` is a groove with a **clear** pane in it, deliberately not the gradient — that tile belongs to `PlSegmentedButton`. The indicator animates `left`/`top`/`width`/`height` from Base UI's `--active-tab-*`, never a transform.
- [PlAccordion](https://plass.cdget.com/components/surfaces/accordion): A stack of sections that fold open one at a time, built on Base UI's Accordion. `PlAccordion` holds the stack and `PlAccordionItem` is one fold; `size`, `density` and `dividers` are inherited from the stack rather than set per item. `variant` defaults to `glass` and is read the way a container reads it — `solid` is the densest clear glass, never a tinted pane, because a sheet holds other people's content and is never dyed. `multiple` lets more than one stay open; `dividers` (on by default) scores the pane instead of tiling it. The panel animates its height from Base UI's measured `--accordion-panel-height`.

### Transitions

- [PlAnimateFade](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-fade): Content arriving or leaving on opacity alone — the plainest effect in the set and the one to reach for first, because nothing moves, so nothing reflows and nothing is resampled. It is also the effect the material already answers on: a Plass sheet is defined by what shows through it, and the glass ladder is itself built out of opacity. `mode="out"` is the same keyframe run backwards rather than a second animation, and it is **held at the end** — a faded-out element stays faded out instead of snapping back when the run finishes. The ten shared settings every `PlAnimate*` takes are here: `duration`, `delay`, `easing`, `repeat` (`'infinite'` rather than `Infinity`, because that word is what reaches CSS), `alternate`, `paused`, `trigger`, `play`, `once` and `threshold`. `trigger` is the interesting one — `mount`, `visible` (paused on its own first frame while it waits, so it is not fully drawn and then blinked out on arrival), `hover` (which starts on focus too, or the effect would be unreachable without a mouse) and `manual`. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the animation is dropped entirely and the content is simply there, which is the opposite of what the loading indicators do and for a reason: a spinner that stops is lying about whether anything is happening, while an entrance that never played has still delivered everything it was carrying.
- [PlAnimateGrow](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-grow): Content unfolding from a point. The difference from a zoom is `origin` and how far it travels: a grow starts close to its final size (`from` defaults to `0.8`) and can be anchored to any edge, so it reads as something opening out of the thing beside it — a panel out of a toolbar, a card out of the row it belongs to. `origin` takes any CSS `transform-origin`, and it governs the standalone `scale` property, which is what lets the effect stay off the `transform` shorthand entirely so a caller's own transform survives. Short travel is also what keeps it safe on glass: a sheet growing from `0.8` stays recognisably the same sheet the whole way. `fade` rides along by default and is worth turning off for something already on the page that is only changing size. It shares its keyframe with `PlAnimateZoom` — the same arithmetic at two strengths, separated by their defaults and their origin rather than by their maths.
- [PlAnimateZoom](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-zoom): Content arriving from the middle of where it will end up — the same arithmetic as `PlAnimateGrow` at more than twice the distance (`from` defaults to `0.4`) and always about the centre, which is the whole difference: a grow unfolds from somewhere, a zoom comes at you. Use it for the one thing on a screen that is meant to interrupt — a confirmation, a result, a number that has just landed. There is deliberately **no `origin`**: a zoom anchored to a corner is a grow, and the library does not offer two spellings of one idea. The travel is long enough to resample text noticeably, so keep it for a figure, a glyph or a small card; a paragraph wants a fade. Nothing repeats by default and this is the effect to leave that way — something that zooms twice is something that failed to arrive the first time.
- [PlAnimateSlide](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-slide): Content travelling in from one edge. `from` is physical — `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` — as `PlassSide` is everywhere in the library, because a panel coming down from the top comes from the top in every writing direction. `distance` defaults to `'100%'`, the element's own width or height, so it starts exactly out of frame and is never half drawn somewhere it does not belong; put it in a box with `overflow: hidden` and the effect is a panel appearing from behind that box's edge. Short distances are a different gesture entirely — a nudge that says something changed rather than an entrance. It moves the element with `translate` rather than changing the layout, so nothing around it reflows while it runs, and `mode="out"` leaves by whichever edge it would have arrived from.
- [PlAnimateReveal](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-reveal): Content uncovered behind a moving edge, and the only entrance in the set where **nothing moves and no colour changes**. A fade changes the ink, a slide changes the position, a grow changes the size; this changes how much of the element is drawn and leaves every pixel it has drawn exactly where it will finally be — which is what makes it the effect for anything whose *position is the information*: a heading over the paragraph it belongs to, a divider between two sections, a chart's plot area, a column of figures that must not be read from the wrong place. It is a `clip-path: inset()` rather than a mask or an `overflow` wrapper, so there is no second element in the layout and nothing reflows; `inset(0)` already means "nothing is cut off", so the to-state is the element's own natural one. `from` is physical — `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` — and `mode="out"` closes from whichever edge it opened towards. **`fade` is off by default**, alone among the effects that offer it: fading a reveal asks for two entrances at once, and the reason to have reached for this one is usually that the first was the problem.
- [PlAnimateRotate](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-rotate): Content turning about a point. **Two angles rather than one**, which is what lets a single component be both effects a rotation is ever used for: `from` alone is an arrival — something swings into place and stops — while `from={0} to={360}` with `repeat="infinite"` and `easing="linear"` is a spin that never lands, which is what a badge, a loading mark or a decorative glyph wants. Turn `fade` off for the second, or the repeat reads as flickering. `origin` takes any CSS `transform-origin`, so turning about a corner is a hinge rather than a wheel. Rotation is the one movement the design language allows on a glyph without argument — a chevron is turned rather than redrawn all over the library — and it is **not for text**, which is resampled along its whole length. If the turning is what says something is happening, `PlProgressCircular` is the component: it slows under `prefers-reduced-motion` rather than stopping, and this one stops.
- [PlAnimateBlink](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-blink): Content pulsing between full opacity and a floor. The cycle is **symmetric** — full, faint, full — so however many times it runs it ends where it started; a blink that finished halfway would leave the element permanently half drawn, which reads as a rendering fault rather than as an effect that ended. `repeat` defaults to `'infinite'` here and to `1` everywhere else, because a single blink is a flicker and nobody asks for a flicker. `min` is how faint it gets at the bottom, and it is worth raising for anything that has to stay readable while it pulses. There is no `mode` and no `fade`: a blink is a cycle rather than an arrival, so it has no direction to run in. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` it is dropped entirely and the content sits at full opacity — so `min` must never be the only thing carrying the message.
- [PlAnimateAppear](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-appear): A list of things settling into place one after another. Each child takes the same short drift and fade held back by its position, so the effect belongs to the **set** rather than to any one item, and a reader's eye is walked down the list in the order it should be read. The animation is written **onto the children themselves** rather than onto wrappers around them — a row of `<li>`s stays a row of `<li>`s, a grid's cells stay its direct children, and the class and style each child already had are kept alongside; only a bare string, which has no element to write onto, is wrapped in a `<span>`. `stagger` counts **children**, not leaves: eight children are eight steps and one child holding eight things is one step, which is also how to opt part of a list out. `distance` is short on purpose (`0.75rem`) — this is a settling, not an entrance from off screen. `delay` happens before the first step rather than being added to every child.
- [PlAnimateLighting](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-lighting): A light travelling around the outside of something. The light sits **behind** the content in a stacking context of its own, so what a reader sees is a glow escaping from under the edges — nothing inside is altered, nothing is overlaid, and it works on a `PlCard` or a `PlButton` without touching how they are drawn. The arc **turns between the two ends of the family** as it travels, which is the same rule every filled surface in the library follows: a flat coloured arc would be paint, and nothing here is paint. What moves is the `from` angle of a conic gradient — only animatable because the angle is a registered custom property with a type; rotating the pseudo-element instead swings its corners out past the element on every quarter turn. `arc`, `blur` and `spread` are the shape of the light: small arc is a spark, large is a sweep, and `blur={0}` stops being light and becomes a graphic. **`size` has to agree with the radius of what is inside**, or the glow cuts a corner the content has already rounded away. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the arc stops travelling and becomes an even glow.
- [PlAnimateMarquee](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-marquee): Content scrolling steadily past, forever. The content is laid down **twice**, and each copy travels exactly its own length plus the gap — so the moment the first copy has left, the second is standing precisely where it began: no seam, no jump, no frame where the strip is empty, and none of it depends on measuring anything, because a percentage `translate` resolves against the element's own box. What *is* measured is the **speed**: `speed` is pixels per second rather than a duration, so a strip of four logos and a strip of forty move at a reader's pace instead of the long one becoming a blur, and it is re-measured whenever the strip changes size. `pauseOnHover` is on by default and is not decoration — content moving past a pointer cannot be clicked reliably, and a link inside a marquee that never stops is a link nobody can follow. **Only the first copy is read out**; the rest carry `aria-hidden`, or a screen reader would announce the strip as many times as it was laid down.
- [PlAnimateHeadline](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-headline): One line replacing the one above it, on a timer. Every line sits in the **same grid cell**, so the box is as tall as the longest of them from the first frame and never resizes as the reel turns — which is the whole difficulty with this effect, and the reason the lines that are not showing keep their space with `visibility` rather than being taken out of the layout. It is deliberately **not a ticker**: a line comes up, it stops, and `interval` is counted from the moment it *arrives* rather than from the start of the cycle, so raising `duration` does not quietly eat the reading time. Passing `index` makes it controlled and stops it running a timer of its own, because a controlled headline is somebody else's clock and a second one underneath it would fight for the same state. It is **not for content a reader has to see** — there is no guarantee anyone is looking during the two seconds a line is up, and a screen reader is given whichever line happens to be showing rather than the set.
- [PlAnimateTyping](https://plass.cdget.com/components/transitions/animate-typing): Text appearing one character at a time. The whole string is in the document from the first frame — in a clipped box a screen reader reads **once**, never made to sit through the performance — and what animates is a visible copy that is `aria-hidden`. So the effect costs a reader who cannot see it nothing, and costs a reader who can nothing either: the box is not laid out from the characters that have arrived, so the text around it does not reflow on every frame. The advance is by **grapheme** rather than by code point, via `Intl.Segmenter`: `👩‍👩‍👧` is one character to a reader and seven code points to JavaScript. `speed` is characters per second and is the natural unit — a long paragraph and a short one should be typed at the same pace, not in the same time — while `duration`, if given, is the time for the whole string and overrides it. `repeat`, `hold` and `erase` make it a loop; without `erase` a repeat clears in one frame, which is right for a line being replaced rather than rewritten. **Only text is typed** — an element among the children contributes its text and nothing about its markup, because there is no honest way to reveal half of a link.

## Hooks

React-only, and the machinery the library already ran on rather than anything new. Available from the barrel and from `plass-ui/hooks`. Flutter's answers to the same questions are framework calls (`MediaQuery`, `PlassTheme`) rather than anything this package would add, and each page names them.

- [usePlMediaQuery](https://plass.cdget.com/hooks/use-media-query): Whether the window matches a CSS media query, as a boolean that re-renders when the answer changes — `usePlMediaQuery('(pointer: coarse)')`. `useSyncExternalStore` rather than an effect and a `useState`, which matters for one reason: it has a **server snapshot**, and that snapshot is `false`. So the answer on the server and through the hydrating render is `false`, and the real one arrives in the render after — which is why the library's own components pair the hook with a CSS class rather than replacing one with the other, and why anything that has to be right in the *first* frame belongs in a Tailwind variant. Reach for it when the decision is one CSS cannot make: whether a component is mounted at all (`display: none` still builds the subtree, still runs its effects and still fetches), how many rows to request, which branch a handler takes. One `MediaQueryList` is kept per query string and shared, so twenty responsive components install one listener. It asks the same engine the stylesheet asks, so `(width >= 48rem)` here and `md:` in a class change at the same moment — including when the reader has enlarged their root font size, which a measured `innerWidth` gets wrong.
- [usePlBreakpoint](https://plass.cdget.com/hooks/use-breakpoint): Which rung of the ladder the window is on (`'xs' | 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl'`), and `usePlBreakpointValue` for the value a `PlassResponsive<T>` map resolves to there. The ladder is Tailwind's own — 40rem, 48rem, 64rem, 80rem, with `xs` from zero — so a decision made in JavaScript and a decision made in a class name change together. The map is the same shape and the same rule as a responsive prop on `PlGrid`: a bare value applies everywhere, a map applies each entry **from its own breakpoint up**, and an entry cascades to the rungs above it, so `{ xs: 1, md: 3 }` is a whole layout. Below every rung the map named it is **`undefined`** rather than a guess. It is four media queries rather than one `innerWidth` read, because the ladder is written in `rem` and a reader who has changed their default font size would otherwise get a rung that disagrees with the stylesheet. `xs` is the server's answer and the first one a browser renders, which is also the safe one.
- [usePlReducedMotion](https://plass.cdget.com/hooks/use-reduced-motion): Whether the reader has asked their platform for less movement, as `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` read through the same store. The library already answers it everywhere it moves — every keyframe in the stylesheet is switched off at once — and this is the same answer for the motion an application writes itself, where there is no rule to switch off: a `scrollIntoView` that should not smooth, a number that should land rather than count up. **"Reduced" is not "none", and the library's own components disagree with each other on purpose**: an entrance is dropped entirely, because an animation that never played has still delivered everything it was carrying, while a loading indicator is *slowed* rather than stopped, because a spinner that stopped would be lying about whether anything is still happening. Which of those an effect is, is the question to answer before reaching for this. The server's answer is `false`, which is the safe direction — the preference arrives in the render after hydration, before any of it has had a frame to run in.
- [usePlHotKeys](https://plass.cdget.com/hooks/use-hot-keys): Keyboard chords bound outside any one control — `usePlHotKeys({ 'Mod+K': open, 'Mod+S': save })`. The map is the same `PlassHotKeys` a field's `hotKeys` prop takes and the chords are spelled the way `PlHotKeys` draws them, which is the whole point: a shortcut that is **displayed** and a shortcut that is **bound** are one string rather than two that drift. `PlCommandPalette` is the first caller — it has bound its own opener this way since it existed, with a private copy of the matcher. Three rules, shared with the prop: a modifier is checked in **both** directions (`Enter` does not fire on `Shift+Enter`), a chord that matches is **consumed** so the browser's own `Mod+K` does not also open, and an event that is *already* consumed is left alone — a field's binding wins over a page's. `whileTyping` is off by default and is narrower than it sounds: a chord carrying `Mod`/`Ctrl`/`Meta`/`Alt` is answered in a field anyway (none can appear in its value), and so is a key that does nothing there — `Escape` above all, since a panel that closes on Escape has to close from inside its own form. What is held back is a printable character or an editing key, which is exactly the `/`-eats-the-URL case. Handlers are read fresh on every keystroke, so an inline object literal costs nothing and a handler closing over current state is never stale; what rebinds is the **set of chords**. `target` scopes it to an element or a ref (a `keydown` only reaches an element containing the focus), and `enabled: false` removes the listener rather than muting the handler.
- [usePlColorScheme](https://plass.cdget.com/hooks/use-color-scheme): The dark mode toggle, plus `PlColorSchemeScript` for the flash. A page that only follows the platform needs neither — the tokens answer `prefers-color-scheme` on their own — and this is for the app that offers a **choice**, which needs three things CSS cannot do: somewhere to keep it, something to write it onto `<html>`, and a way to paint it before the first frame. `scheme` is what the reader chose and **`system` is the absence of a choice rather than a third theme**: it removes the attribute and hands the question back, so the page follows the platform again rather than being pinned to the platform's current answer. `resolved` is what is painted. `toggle` flips from what is *painted*, so the first press on a system-dark page gives light. It writes the `data-theme` attribute **and** the class, not as belt and braces: the attribute is what this library's tokens read and the class is what a consumer's own Tailwind `dark:` utilities read. `PlColorSchemeScript` goes in `<head>` with `suppressHydrationWarning` on `<html>`; it renders nothing but a `<script>`, calls no hook and reads no context, so it stays a **server component** — a client component here would arrive with the bundle and be too late by definition. `storageKey` and `defaultScheme` are read **once**, when the first component using that key mounts, which is what makes two toggles on one page agree. A second tab that changes the scheme changes this one. The stylesheet now also sets `color-scheme`, so scrollbars, the caret and native popups switch with the page.
